items.canonical_answer: Intestinal enzymes need a less acidic environment; raising pH towards their suitable range supports their activity.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: intestinal enzymes work best in less acidic conditions.
1 mark: because neutralising the acid raises the pH towards their optimum, their activity increases.

items.prompt: A student says that bile is an acid that adds to the acidity of the food in the stomach. Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: Bile is made in the liver and enters the small intestine, not the stomach; it is alkaline and helps neutralise the acid from the stomach, so it raises the pH instead of lowering it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error is that bile is not acidic: it is alkaline.
1 mark: bile enters the small intestine, not the stomach, and neutralises the stomach acid there instead, raising the pH.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.

items.prompt: Outline how bile helps fat digestion without itself being an enzyme.
items.canonical_answer: Bile emulsifies fat into small droplets; this increases surface area; lipase then has more surface on which to digest fat.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names emulsification: bile salts break fat into small droplets.
1 mark: the droplets have a larger total surface area.
1 mark: lipase can then reach more fat, so it digests the fat faster. Bile is not an enzyme and does not digest the fat.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.

items.prompt: Explain why emulsification is not the same as chemical digestion.
items.canonical_answer: Droplets become smaller without fat molecules being chemically broken down; lipase is still needed to produce digestion products.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: emulsification only breaks fat into smaller droplets, while the fat molecules stay unchanged.
1 mark: lipase is still needed because chemical digestion breaks the fat molecules into fatty acids and glycerol.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.

items.prompt: Describe a complete investigation of the emulsifying effect of bile salts on oil.
items.canonical_answer: Change bile-salt presence using equal added solution volumes; measure separation after a fixed time; keep oil/water volumes, tube type and shaking the same; shake matched tubes with and without bile salts then observe separation at set times; repeat each treatment and compare results.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the independent variable is changed: bile salts are added to one tube and an equal volume of water to the other.
1 mark: the dependent variable is measured: how far the oil and water separate, or how cloudy they stay, after a set time.
1 mark: at least two of oil volume, water volume, tube size, shaking time and temperature are kept the same.
1 mark: a workable method: shake both tubes in the same way, then observe them at set times.
1 mark: repeats each treatment and compares the results, for example the mean separation time.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.

items.prompt: Suggest a limitation and an improvement if one bile-salt tube is shaken for 60 s but the no-bile tube for 10 s.
items.canonical_answer: Different shaking can itself change dispersion; shake both for the same measured duration and intensity.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the limitation is that longer shaking could itself break the oil into finer droplets, so the difference may not be caused by the bile salts.
1 mark: an improvement: shake both tubes for the same measured time and with the same force.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.

items.prompt: Suggest what is supported when replicated tubes containing oil, water and bile salts remain dispersed after 5 min, while matched oil-and-water controls separate. No lipase was added.
items.canonical_answer: Bile salts help maintain small dispersed oil droplets; the result supports emulsification, not chemical digestion because lipase and product tests are absent.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the oil stays as fine droplets with bile salts but separates in the controls, so bile salts keep the fat emulsified.
1 mark: this shows emulsification, not chemical digestion, because no lipase was added and no products were tested for.

items.prompt: Identify the main region for absorption of digested food and the structure on its lining that increases surface area.
items.canonical_answer: Small intestine; villi.

items.prompt: Describe how villi change the absorbing surface of the small intestine.
items.canonical_answer: Numerous projections extend into the lumen; together they greatly increase the internal surface area.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names the structure: many finger-like projections (villi) extend into the lumen.

items.prompt: Explain why many villi make absorption more effective than a smooth lining of the same tube length.
items.canonical_answer: They expose more epithelial surface to digested food; more nutrient molecules can cross at the same time.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: more absorbing surface is exposed to the digested food.

items.prompt: Describe the transport structures inside a villus and their different roles.
items.canonical_answer: Blood capillaries receive sugars and amino acids; the central lacteal receives absorbed lipid material.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names the blood capillaries, which take up sugars and amino acids.

items.prompt: State the role of the hepatic portal vein after nutrient absorption.
items.canonical_answer: It carries nutrient-rich blood from the intestines to the liver.

items.prompt: Describe how the liver stores excess glucose and later makes it available.
items.canonical_answer: It converts glucose into glycogen; glycogen can later be broken down to release glucose.

items.prompt: Explain why storing excess glucose as glycogen is useful between meals.
items.canonical_answer: Storage builds a reserve after absorption; later breakdown supplies glucose when little is entering from the intestine.

items.prompt: Describe how the liver handles excess amino acids.
items.canonical_answer: It deaminates them; the nitrogen-containing part is converted to urea for excretion.

items.prompt: Explain why excess absorbed amino acids lead to increased urea production.
items.canonical_answer: Excess amino acids cannot be stored, so in the liver deamination removes the amino group (the nitrogen-containing part) and this is converted into urea.

items.prompt: Explain why fat is useful as a longer-term energy reserve.
items.canonical_answer: It stores much chemical energy relative to its mass; it can be broken down to supply respiratory fuel when intake is insufficient.
